figures.label: fig:qos_score_validation
figures.caption: Comparison of failure impact under increased input rates. Static leads to sustained QoS degradation, while stop-and-restart introduces disruption. The figure highlights the need to bound both degradation duration and recovery overhead.

figures.label: fig:architecture
figures.caption: Overview of BoundGuard. The system detects sustained QoS violations and performs validation-driven candidate evaluation to bound the duration of ineffective placements without a system-wide pause}.

figures.label: fig:bounded_recovery
figures.caption: Breakdown of recovery latency into detection delay and post-detection phases. Detection remains stable, while total recovery remains below the analytical upper bound (33 s) instantiated from $T + N_{cand}(T_v + \delta) + T_{stable}$, despite increasing interference.

figures.label: fig:runtime_overhead
figures.caption: Steady-state overhead under stable execution. BoundGuard introduces negligible latency and CPU overhead.

figures.label: fig:detection_sensitivity
figures.caption: Sensitivity to detection parameters $(T, \epsilon)$. Detection latency increases with the monitoring window and remains bounded by it, while recovery behavior remains stable.

figures.label: fig:q13-persistence
figures.caption: Recovery outcome (left) and, for the methods that recover, how long the violation lasts (right). Static never returns below $\epsilon$ on either platform, so it has no persistence to report and does not appear in the right panel; its terminal violation is shown on the left instead.}

figures.label: fig:q13-cumulative
figures.caption: Cumulative QoS violation $\int V(t) dt$ over the same runs.}

figures.label: fig:fluid_validation
figures.caption: Fluid recovery model vs.\ measurement. (a) Accumulation slope tracks $\lambda-\mu_{cpu}$; (b) drain slope tracks $-(\mu^{\ast}-\lambda)$; (c) the drain slope tends to zero as $\lambda\to\mu^{\ast}$, reproducing the predicted divergence of $T_{stable}$.

figures.label: fig:b2
figures.caption: Buffer sweep ($\beta_B\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5\}$): $p99$ end-to-end latency (top) and dropped frames (bottom) on both platforms. The ordering of methods is stable across buffer sizes; the buffer changes only whether excess arrivals surface as drops or as late completions.

figures.label: fig:dynamic_adaptation
figures.caption: Adaptation under a workload increase on both platforms. Static remains in persistent violation; BoundGuard offloads and returns below the threshold.}

figures.label: fig:misprediction
figures.caption: QoS behavior under ML misprediction. All methods initially follow the same ML-selected placement, but only BoundGuard performs a second transition after validation, recovering to a stable configuration, while other methods remain in sustained violation.

figures.label: fig:bounded
figures.caption: Behavior when no candidate satisfies the constraint. BoundGuard rejects all five, reverts to the best it observed, and ends below the baselines; the search interval is marked.}

figures.label: fig:budget-rank
figures.caption: Worst-case persistence $T+N_{cand}(T_v+\delta)$ over the candidate budget, instantiated with a single representative transition cost ($\delta=1$ s, the measured in-place vision swap). The shaded region is where a recovering placement at rank $k^{\ast}$ is reachable ($k^{\ast}\le N_{cand}$); the markers are the two measured operating points. Q3 sits on the boundary, and the two-generative-model case sits outside it. Because a single $\delta$ is used throughout, the surface is a lower envelope: instantiating per transition raises it wherever a candidate requires relocating a generative model ($\delta\approx2.9$ s), which is why the Q3 bound quoted above is $24$--$26$ s rather than the $23$ s shown here. The map is analytic---it evaluates the bound rather than reporting runs---and is included to show the trade a larger budget imposes.}

figures.label: fig:npu_violation
figures.caption: Misprediction recovery on the CPU--NPU platform. The predictor's top-ranked placement keeps the background LLM on the NPU, where it contends with the foreground vision applications; only BoundGuard rejects it and recovers.}

figures.label: fig:c2-ablation
figures.caption: Violation trajectories under misprediction for the four corners of the ablation. BoundGuard returns below $\epsilon$; removing dwell leaves the system at a high violation level, while removing progress leaves it pinned just above $\epsilon$ on the top-ranked placement.}
